scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: every response this page's reads receive carries the envelope shape its client expects
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 4 read relation(s), 1 were probed live at the gateway (logbook).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed: a page writing two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them, so a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between them leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page writing one table and letting a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic BY CONSTRUCTION, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants checked against live data and ALL HOLD. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ★ROSTER: {"client-sequenced": 11, "single-or-no-write": 11}. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT green even though nothing is broken today. It writes logbook + schedule_items and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC writing both - so a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. Every declared invariant holds against live data, which is genuinely reassuring, but 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code; banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. ★RE-WALKED AFTER THIS SESSION'S TWELVE PRODUCT FIXES so the evidence carries digests of the code as it now stands - R4b expired the prior rows because the fixes changed the very functions they rested on. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

control.note: the trigger handle_community_post_xp writes the award ledger, so a detector that cannot see this link cannot see any link

evidence.asserts: A multi-row or multi-table write either lands whole or not at all; a half-applied write is visible as an inconsistency in the ledger. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - write_atomicity exercises every declared ledger invariant live, inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK, and checks that the paired halves of a write cannot come apart.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every declared ledger invariant holds against the live database, exercised transactionally rather than reasoned about. The exposure the gate reports rather than hides is the honest part: 11 pages sequence TWO writes client-side, which is structural risk (a tab closed between them leaves the second undone) and is recorded as exposure, not counted as a failure, because no half-write has actually occurred in the data. That distinction is the same one this platform learned the hard way from a one-sided ledger write that passed every guard - the difference between "this could come apart" and "this has come apart" decides whether you are hardening a path or repairing rows. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration or function under this claim still expires it, and replay re-earns it in one command instead of a browser session.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes logbook + schedule_items and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

findings.detail: SAYS NOTHING AT EITHER SAMPLE, with 10 intercepted requests - i.e. the whole Supabase surface failing. No [role=alert], [role=status], [aria-live], toast, error, notice or banner element carried any failure wording at ~1.3s or ~10s. It also keeps the 'Live · refreshed on load' chip up and renders the word CLEAR while blind, so the reader gets a positive all-clear on a plan built from data that never arrived - the same shape as inventory's 'STOCKED / every part above its reorder point'. Three zeros persist at both samples. WHY THIS IS THE WORST OF THE THREE SHAPES FOUND IN THIS COHORT: community answers '✕ Could not load posts' at both samples and project-manager at least says 'Load failed' once, so the platform demonstrably HAS the vocabulary and the containers - this page simply never reaches for them. From the reader's side a caught-and-swallowed error is indistinguishable from a server that honestly answered nothing, which is the exact clause this oracle exists to test. || METHOD: WHOLE-SURFACE INJECTION, SAMPLED TWICE. Every /rest/v1/, /functions/v1/ and /rpc/ request is answered 500 {code:500,message:...} with /auth/v1/ deliberately left alive so the identity guard can still read a valid session; interceptions are COUNTED and a verdict over zero is refused as vacuous; the surface is read at ~1.3s and again ~10s later. THE SECOND SAMPLE IS THE POINT: the failure notice on several of these pages is a toast that auto-dismisses, so a single-instant reading of this oracle is not reproducible - which is why an earlier pass on this bank recorded 'says nothing on failure' across 11 of 16 pages, RETRACTED it as a <main>-scoped lens artefact, and a later pass recorded 12 of 12 passing. Sampling twice shows how both happened. POSITIVE CONTROL, same lens, same run: community's '✕ Could not load posts' and analytics' 'Analysis failed, check console' were caught at BOTH samples, so a silent reading is the page's silence rather than the lens's blindness - the check the retracted finding lacked. Guarded on identity and on pathname, so a session drop or a bounce to the landing page refuses instead of reading a shell.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - fail_401: an expired session is not surfaced honestly on this page. THIS FAILS ON 17 OF 17 PAGES WALKED, and the fix is ADOPTION, not a new message
findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Injecting a 401 into this page's reads, the page does not tell the reader their session expired, does not name the session as the cause, and does not state the consequence for what they were doing. THE REFLEX IS TO WRITE THE MISSING MESSAGE AND THAT WOULD BE WRONG - it already exists. utils.js:1568 reads 'Your session expired, so nothing was saved. Sign in again and redo this step.' and :1611 has the read equivalent, with _WH_PG_DENIAL at :1518 and a careful 401-versus-403 note beneath it. There is even a comment recording that this was fixed once on the inquiry path, where a 42501 told a SIGNED-IN buyer their session had expired, and that 'the shared helper kept the bug for every other path'. Writing a new string would add a second source of truth for text that is already correct. SO THE DEFECT IS ADOPTION: the read path catches the status and never renders whReadError's text. A uniform 17-of-17 failure is not seventeen independent lapses, it is one shared path swallowing the status - which means ONE fix earns all seventeen rows in a single sweep. Same shape as the other platform-wide finds in this arc: ::placeholder absent everywhere, companion-launcher.js with no prefers-reduced-motion block at all. AND THE PROBE IS NOT AT FAULT, which matters before acting on a 17/17 result: fail_null_field passes on 16 of 16 pages under the same injection harness. A broken probe does not pass one injection everywhere and fail another everywhere. Row stays owed; measure adoption at the point of RENDER, not by the helper's existence.

findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_timeout failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. That contradiction is what exposed the scope bug. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. WHAT SURVIVES: the fail_401 finding was REAL. Before the central fix there was no session notice on any page at all - no element existed to be missed - so 12 of 12 pages genuinely told a reader nothing when their session died, and the fix at getDb() is what created the notice they now show. That one is not withdrawn. Only the timeout and partial claims are, and they are withdrawn in full. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THIS ARC KEEPS RE-LEARNING: an instrument that measures the wrong REGION produces well-formed readings, and a uniform failure across many pages should raise suspicion of the probe before it is written up as a platform defect. The same lens-scope error once measured 15 of 518 nodes for contrast because it scoped to <main> while the report mounted outside it.

findings.title: RETRACTION SUPERSEDED - the withdrawal above rested on a contaminated reading; fail_partial genuinely FAILS here (9 of 12 pages), reinstated
findings.detail: THE RETRACTION ON THIS ROW WAS ITSELF WRONG, and this note supersedes it. Three measurements of fail_partial exist and only the middle one is contaminated: (1) FIRST READ, text scope = <main>: failed on 13 of 16 pages. (2) SECOND READ, after I widened the scope to include body-level notice regions: passed on 12 of 12 - and on the strength of that I retracted the finding on 12 pages, writing that 'the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf'. (3) THIRD READ, after I made my own 401 notice CLEAR ITSELF: fails on 9 of 12. NOTHING ON ANY PARTIAL CODE PATH CHANGED ACROSS THOSE THREE. What changed in (2) is that the central session notice I had just added to getDb() was still pinned to the page from the 401 injection earlier in the same failures() run, so namesTheFailure was matching MY OWN leftover text - 'Your session expired, so this page could not be loaded' - rather than anything the page said about a truncated payload. Reading (1) and reading (3) AGREE with each other; (2) is the outlier, and (2) is the one I acted on. SO THE ORIGINAL FINDING STANDS, at 9 of 12 rather than 13 of 16: on this page a truncated payload is rendered without the reader being told part of the data is missing. The withdrawal note above should be read as evidence about my instrument's history, not as an exoneration of this page. WHY THIS HAPPENED, because the mechanism matters more than the count: I fixed one artefact (a main-scoped text read) and in the same window introduced another (a notice that outlived its injection), then used a measurement taken between the two to overturn a finding. A correction is only as good as the reading behind it, and a reading taken while another fix is half-landed is not a baseline. The rule I keep re-deriving: change ONE thing, re-measure, and never let a retraction rest on a single run - especially not one that flips a uniform FAIL into a uniform PASS, which is the same too-good-to-be-true signature that should raise suspicion of the instrument in either direction.

findings.detail: FAILS, AND IT FAILS THROUGH THE FIX I LANDED EARLIER TODAY - recorded against my own work rather than left for someone else to trip over. The fail_500 fix on this page routes a failed read into the rendered STATE (an em-dash sentinel, tag UNKNOWN, a verdict that names the failure) and it is verified for that case. OFFLINE IS A DIFFERENT FAILURE MODE AND IT IS NOT COVERED. MEASURED: fetch was made to REJECT (Promise.reject(new TypeError('Failed to fetch'))) for every /rest/v1/, /functions/v1/ and /rpc/ request while leaving /auth/v1/ alive, with navigator.onLine forced false - i.e. a real no-network condition rather than a server answering badly. 13-19 requests blocked per page, so the perturbation is not marginal. Result on all four pages measured (inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, logbook): every KPI reads **0**, ZERO sentinels rendered, and the verdict is frozen at its initial placeholder - 'Computing stock health...', 'Loading day plan...', 'Computing PM compliance...' - which will never resolve. inventory additionally still shows CLEAR / STOCKED wording. THE ROOT, PRECISELY: my flags are set from `res.error` - a RESOLVED response carrying an error body. A rejected promise never produces one, so the flag stays false and the guard I added never runs; worse, the rejection propagates and aborts the init chain before the summary renders at all, which is why the verdict keeps its HTML placeholder instead of even reaching the zero branch. A 500 and a dead network arrive through two different doors and I only instrumented one. THIS IS ALSO THE STUCK-PLACEHOLDER SHAPE the same session found on skillmatrix (a persistent, correct failure toast beside a verdict reading 'Computing skill progress...' forever): nothing false is ASSERTED by a frozen 'Computing...', so an oracle hunting fabricated values passes it while a person watches a spinner that will never finish. Here it is worse, because the KPIs underneath it read 0. A toast does say 'check your connection' on these pages, so the reader is not told nothing - but the same timing evidence from this session applies: toasts on these pages fire within 150-240ms and dismiss, while the zeros persist indefinitely. TO FINISH (batched per A15, one wave, no mid-walk edits): set the same _<x>ReadFailed flag in the CATCH block each of these load functions already has (inventory.html:2214 'inventory load failed', and the equivalents on the other three), and CALL the summary renderer from that catch so the sentinel path runs even when the load threw. Then re-walk fail_offline AND fail_timeout together, since a timeout arrives through the same rejection door.

subject.name: an offline delete of a never-synced item drains cleanly

seen.ref: PDDA Y1b adopter #2: offline delete queues op:'delete', probe PASS

scenarios.oracle: an offline delete of a never-synced item drains cleanly rather than 0-row-no-op'ing forever

evidence.asserts: THIS WAS BROKEN AND IS NOW FIXED - the oracle named the exact failure and it was live. Deleting an item created offline collapses onto the same keyPath id, so the drain sends a delete for a row that never reached the server; PostgREST returns 0 rows; and the shared queue set `unconfirmed = true` for ANY 0-row result. The item was therefore never removed, retry_count climbed to MAX_RETRIES, and the row was marked `stalled` - the widget reporting permanently STUCK work for an operation that had in fact succeeded. dayplanner's own comment asserted the drain 'no-ops harmlessly on the absent row'; the shared queue it delegates to did not agree. Zero rows means opposite things for the two ops: for an UPDATE it means the write did not land and the payload is still the worker's only copy; for a DELETE it usually means the requested end state is already true. The one ambiguity worth keeping is an RLS refusal, which also returns 0 rows while the row still exists - so the fix separates them by asking whether this identity can still SEE the row. Absent means the delete's goal holds and it drains; still visible means it really was refused and the backoff still surfaces it. The fix is in the SHARED queue, so the same stuck-item class is closed for asset-hub, inventory and logbook too.
evidence.checked: Proven by A/B on one probe rather than by reading the diff: the identical script was run against git HEAD's offline-queue.js and against the fixed file, so the change in behaviour is attributable to the edit and nothing else. Both files were syntax-checked, and the baseline parsed too - so the pre-fix reading is a real behaviour, not a broken build. Probe rows removed and the queue re-read to its starting depth.

subject.name: a planning collision is refused with a reason

scenarios.oracle: two supervisors planning the same worker's hour: one write wins, the other is refused with a reason - never a silent last-write-wins

evidence.asserts: The race was real and SILENT, and the silence is what got fixed. Measured in psql: two writers upsert the same schedule_items id and the second simply replaces the first - 'A: pump inspection' became 'B: motor alignment' with no error, no version check and no refusal. There is no constraint that could have caught it (only a PK on the client-generated text id) and no version column. THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS THE WRONG ONE. An updated_at optimistic lock is exactly what this platform reserves for online-only writes, because schedule_items is QUEUE-BACKED (wh_dayplanner_offline): a queued edit drains carrying a stale version, so a lock would conflict on every drain and would take away the offline capture a technician in a basement depends on - the same trap as adopting an online-only refusal on a queue-backed write. So last-write-wins stays, and the oracle's real demand - never a SILENT last-write-wins - is met on the surface: when a remote change lands on the very item this person has open, the existing realtime channel names it rather than reloading the list underneath them. Separately confirmed NOT a defect: two DIFFERENT items on one worker's hour both persist, which is deliberate - the page's layoutBlocks() renders overlapping blocks side by side.
evidence.checked: The race itself proven in psql inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK as ROLE authenticated with jwt claims, then re-counted to confirm 0 probe rows survived. The fix proven with TWO REAL CONTEXTS rather than a simulation: a signed-in browser holding the item open in its editor, and a genuinely separate writer updating that row, with the notice read WHILE IT WAS ON SCREEN - a first read at 6s reported shown:false purely because the toast auto-hides at 3000ms, so the poll was tightened rather than the result accepted. The showToast call was also corrected before this run: its signature is (msg, type), not (msg, ms), and passing a duration would have repeated a known bug where a numeric second argument produced a toast displayed for zero milliseconds. The touched row was restored to its original title afterwards.

evidence.asserts: every quantity a reader could act on carries its unit; a bare number is either a count of things or prints its own denominator
evidence.checked: SETTLED BY READING EVERY FLAGGED FIGURE INDIVIDUALLY, after TWO generations of automated classifier both failed - which is why this row rests on inspection with a stated denominator rather than on a lens verdict. GEN-1 FAILED FIVE WAYS and was discarded: it flagged wizard STEP ORDINALS (1 2 3) as unit-less quantities; it lacked bare 'h' and 'year' in its vocabulary, so analytics' CORRECT 6.2h MTTR and 1-year window were called bare; it flagged BOUNDED SCORES that print their own denominator (hive readiness 62/100); and its fixed 3-level ancestor walk escaped the label region entirely, returning the PAGE TITLE as a figure's context on dayplanner. GEN-2 walks up only until a label-bearing ancestor is found and ABSTAINS when none exists (24 abstentions on dayplanner, 21 on analytics), exempts ordinals and printed-denominator scores, and widened the unit vocabulary. THEN EVERY REMAINING FLAG WAS READ BY HAND and confirmed dimensionless: '30 machines', '3 low' / '0 out', hive readiness sub-scores 100/42/70, 'Mechanical - 3 +' skill level, and per-asset failure counts (CR-001 11, GEN-001 10). THE REASON NO LENS CAN CLOSE THIS ORACLE: 'is this number dimensionless?' is a judgement about the DOMAIN, not a lexical property of the label. '30 machines' needs no unit because a machine is a thing rather than a quantity of something; '2.438' NEEDS one because vibration is measured in mm/s or in g and those differ by orders of magnitude. A keyword lens cannot make that distinction, and one that claims to is producing confident noise. THE CONTRAST WORTH RECORDING: a sweep across these pages found nothing they got wrong, while careful reading of ONE panel found the thing that matters - asset-hub renders 2.438 under a VIBRATION heading with no unit, even though v_sensor_truth carries a unit column beside value. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 8 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 5 reads answered 500, **this page offers no retry control at all** - zero visible elements whose label or handler mentions retry or try-again. Its failure messaging is otherwise good - 'Could not load your plan. This is a connection problem, not an empty day. Reload to see your items.' with `dp-today-hero`, `dp-week-hero` and `dp-overdue-hero` dashed - though the open-items panel still reads '0 open items from Logbook' and 'No open items'. SO A READER'S ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL PAGE RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant means losing whatever was on screen and paying the whole load again on the connection that just failed. THE PLATFORM HAS THE PATTERN ALREADY, so this is unadopted rather than undesigned: community renders a toast reading 'Couldn't load the community feed. Check your connection and try again.' with a **Retry** button beside it, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 posts. Six of the seven pages measured in this sweep have neither. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that re-issues the failed read and is measurable as such - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That distinction is not hypothetical: it is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY FAILING EVERY READ AT window.fetch AND COUNTING WHAT THE PAGE DOES NEXT. findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). findings.title: FAILS THE FIRST CLAUSE ONLY, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' Two clauses, and this page is measured against both. MEASURED with 5 reads answered 500: this page
findings.detail: FAILS THE FIRST CLAUSE ONLY, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' Two clauses, and this page is measured against both. MEASURED with 5 reads answered 500: this page DOES say the primary is down, in domain language - **'Could not load your plan. This is a connection problem, not an empty day. Reload to see your items.'** - and it dashes its tiles rather than zeroing them (`dp-today-hero`, `dp-week-hero` and `dp-overdue-hero` all read a dash). So it does not pretend nothing happened, and that half is genuinely done. WHAT IS MISSING IS THE FALLBACK ITSELF, and no page-level fix can supply it: THERE IS NO READ FALLBACK ON THIS PLATFORM, AND THAT IS PROVEN FROM THE SERVICE WORKER'S SOURCE RATHER THAN INFERRED. `sw.js` handles API traffic in one branch - `if (url.includes('supabase.co') || url.includes('fonts.goog') ...) e.respondWith(fetch(e.request).catch(() => new Response('', { status: 503 })))` (sw.js:195-200) - so a failed read resolves to an EMPTY 503 body. And `cache.put` appears **nowhere in the file**, so no API response is ever stored: `caches.match()` cannot hit for a `/rest/v1/` URL because nothing put one there. The 26-entry `SHELL_FILES` precache holds HTML, CSS and JS only. SO THE FIRST CLAUSE CANNOT BE SATISFIED FOR READS BY CONSTRUCTION - there is nothing to engage. The offline layer this platform does have is for WRITES (the `wh_logbook_offline` / `wh_dayplanner_offline` / `wh_assethub_offline` IndexedDB queues), which is a different oracle. That makes the second clause the whole test: does the surface say the primary is down, or does it pretend nothing happened? SO THIS ROW IS NOT A PAGE DEFECT BUT A PLATFORM GAP, recorded here because the oracle asks for a fallback and there is none to engage. It is banked as a finding rather than a pass so the debt stays visible, and rather than `declared-na` because the subject is real - the platform HAS an offline layer, it just serves writes only. NOTE: the open-items panel still reads '0 open items from Logbook' and 'No open items'. WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: cache the last successful read per surface (an IndexedDB mirror beside the existing write queues, or a `cache.put` on the API branch keyed by query) and label the rendered copy with its age - 'showing your last synced copy from 14:20'. That is one central mechanism, not 22 page fixes, which is the CENTRALIZE-FIRST call. MEASURED TWO INDEPENDENT WAYS, so the reading does not rest on one injection style. (1) Every `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request answered with a synthetic 500 at `window.fetch`, `/auth/v1/` left alone so the session survives, interceptions counted and a zero-interception run refused as vacuous. (2) A genuine `setOffline(true)` navigation with the service-worker cache WARM. THE SECOND METHOD TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS TO GET HONEST, WHICH IS WHY IT IS TRUSTWORTHY NOW. Navigating to `/workhive/logbook.html` offline served the branded offline shell every time - not because the page is unavailable offline, but because `SHELL_FILES` precaches ROOT paths (`/logbook.html`) and the `/workhive/` prefix is a different cache key. Measured at the path the cache actually holds, the real page is served. A verdict from the prefixed path would have described a cache miss and called it product behaviour. AND ONE LIMIT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: under Playwright's `setOffline(true)`, `navigator.onLine` still read **true** and `wh-conn-chip` still read 'Online' (hidden). The app's own offline DETECTION therefore never fired, so this reading covers 'the primary is down' but NOT 'the app knows it is offline'. The absence of an offline banner is consequently NOT charged against the page here. A probe that wants that claim must also override `navigator.onLine` and dispatch the `offline` event.

With reads held in flight this page shows explicit loading vocabulary AND 3 dash sentinels (so part of the surface sentinels correctly), while 3
findings.detail: RECORDED OWED WITH A MIXED IN-FLIGHT READING - not passed, not failed, because the evidence genuinely points both ways and one more measurement decides it. With reads held in flight this page shows explicit loading vocabulary AND 3 dash sentinels (so part of the surface sentinels correctly), while 3 bare numbers are on screen, 3 of them zeros. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER THOSE ZEROS ARE ASSERTIONS OR STATIC HTML DEFAULTS. The KPI heroes ship as `0` in the markup and are overwritten when data lands, so a zero seen mid-load may be untouched initial markup rather than a computed claim - and from outside the two are indistinguishable. dayplanner in this same pass showed 3 in-flight zeros against 2 settled zeros, i.e. its zeros were mostly REAL values, which is exactly why a count alone cannot decide. TO FINISH - one targeted probe, no guesswork: snapshot each KPI element's textContent before the reads resolve and again after, and compare against that element's value in the static HTML. A zero that never changes and equals the markup default is a placeholder; a zero written by the render is a fabricated answer. MEASURED BY DELAYING THE PAGE'S OWN READS, NOT BY GUESSING AT A SLOW NETWORK. Every /rest/v1/ and /rpc/ request is wrapped in a 6-second delay before being forwarded to the real fetch (auth left untouched so the identity guard still works), and the surface is read at 2.2s - i.e. WHILE the reads are provably still in flight. Interceptions are COUNTED and a verdict over zero is refused as vacuous. THE ORACLE IS WHETHER A SLOW READ IS SHOWN AS SLOW rather than answered with a fabricated value, so the in-flight state IS the measurement. Three positive signals are collected independently - skeleton/shimmer/aria-busy elements, explicit loading vocabulary in the body, and dash sentinels - alongside the two things that would betray it: how many bare numbers are on screen, and whether any false-empty sentence has appeared. AN HONEST INSTRUMENT LIMIT, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the post-delay sample taken 7s later was still MID-LOAD on three pages (skeletons still present), because 6s per read across sequential reads exceeds that wait. So the settled comparison is NOT used for any verdict here - only the in-flight reading. Using a still-loading sample as the 'after' picture would have made every page look permanently broken.

findings.title: CLASSIFIED WITH EVIDENCE rather than left un-attempted.
findings.detail: CLASSIFIED WITH EVIDENCE rather than left un-attempted. This oracle asks that offline the write be REFUSED before firing and the person told nothing was sent - so before it can be graded, this view's committing write has to be identified and its CLASS settled, because the platform deliberately splits them: field capture QUEUES, while approvals, locked, financial, moderation and role writes are online-only-with-clarity (the generic drain carries no optimistic lock and those writes depend on one). Grading a queue-backed write against a refusal is wrong in both directions - green credits a refusal that must not exist, red calls a working feature a defect. The test is per-FUNCTION, not per-page: inventory, community and skillmatrix each show BOTH classes on one page. See PAGE_TESTBANK_ROADMAP.md SS6 for the sibling offline_queued cell proposed for the queue side, and tools/prove_offline_queued.mjs which grades it. THIS VIEW IS QUEUE-CLASS. Its write is registered with the page's own offline queue (window._whDpQueue over wh_dayplanner_offline, table schedule_items), so offline it is HELD and the person is told it will sync - which is the correct behaviour and the opposite of what this oracle asks for. Refusing it would remove offline capture from someone working with no signal, which is the mistake I made on community's submitPost this session and had to revert after it removed working offline posting. WHAT THIS ROW NEEDS INSTEAD: the offline_queued oracle - zero server writes, POSITIVE acceptance evidence (the queue store grew), the will-sync message, no false refusal wording, and on reconnect a drain that happens EXACTLY ONCE. AND THIS PAGE'S QUEUE CARRIES A PROVEN INVARIANT worth grading with it: an offline create-then-edit must collapse to ONE row (the keyPath/upsert branch), which is this page's own recorded lesson. The week view is a re-bucketing of the same schedule_items the day view writes, so it is the same queued write rather than a second one.

observed.invariant_to_grade_with_it: offline create-then-edit collapses to ONE row (keyPath/upsert)

evidence.checked: NO SUBJECT, and this one is a POSTURE difference rather than an absence: every mutating call on this page targets schedule_items (dayplanner.html:698/745/790) and this page is one of the platform's OFFLINE-QUEUE ADOPTERS - it registers wh_dayplanner_offline. Under the platform rule, field-capture writes QUEUE offline while approvals, locked updates, financial, moderation and role writes are online-only-with-clarity. A queued write is SUPPOSED to be accepted offline and drained later, so demanding that it REFUSE would be demanding the opposite of the designed behaviour. Replacement: the queue behaviour is the offline_queued oracle's subject (drains exactly once, an offline create-then-edit collapses to ONE row), and offline_refusal is graded on the 17 cases across surfaces whose writes are online-only

findings.detail: RECORDED OWED WITH A MIXED IN-FLIGHT READING - not passed, not failed, because the evidence genuinely points both ways and one more measurement decides it. With reads held in flight this page shows explicit loading vocabulary AND 3 dash sentinels (so part of the surface sentinels correctly), while 3 bare numbers are on screen, 3 of them zeros. THE OPEN QUESTION IS WHETHER THOSE ZEROS ARE ASSERTIONS OR STATIC HTML DEFAULTS. The KPI heroes ship as `0` in the markup and are overwritten when data lands, so a zero seen mid-load may be untouched initial markup rather than a computed claim - and from outside the two are indistinguishable. dayplanner in this same pass showed 3 in-flight zeros against 2 settled zeros, i.e. its zeros were mostly REAL values, which is exactly why a count alone cannot decide. TO FINISH - one targeted probe, no guesswork: snapshot each KPI element's textContent before the reads resolve and again after, and compare against that element's value in the static HTML. A zero that never changes and equals the markup default is a placeholder; a zero written by the render is a fabricated answer. MEASURED BY DELAYING THE PAGE'S OWN READS, NOT BY GUESSING AT A SLOW NETWORK. Every /rest/v1/ and /rpc/ request is wrapped in a 6-second delay before being forwarded to the real fetch (auth left untouched so the identity guard still works), and the surface is read at 2.2s - i.e. WHILE the reads are provably still in flight. Interceptions are COUNTED and a verdict over zero is refused as vacuous. THE ORACLE IS WHETHER A SLOW READ IS SHOWN AS SLOW rather than answered with a fabricated value, so the in-flight state IS the measurement. Three positive signals are collected independently - skeleton/shimmer/aria-busy elements, explicit loading vocabulary in the body, and dash sentinels - alongside the two things that would betray it: how many bare numbers are on screen, and whether any false-empty sentence has appeared. AN HONEST INSTRUMENT LIMIT, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: the post-delay sample taken 7s later was still MID-LOAD on three pages (skeletons still present), because 6s per read across sequential reads exceeds that wait. So the settled comparison is NOT used for any verdict here - only the in-flight reading. Using a still-loading sample as the 'after' picture would have made every page look permanently broken.

Fourteen V2 rows across the platform carried a measurement of a view they never visited, which is R7's exact failure: a claim resting on something other than what it names. The count did not move; the evidence did. DECLARED-NA ON A MEASURED DENOMINATOR, NOT AN ASSUMED ONE (rail R10). evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: worker (own-plan boundary) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 1 of its 1 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - logbook (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 4 read relation(s), 1 were probed live at the gateway (logbook).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. evidence.checked: Walked live. THE SECOND HALF DID NOT HOLD, AND WAS FIXED BEFORE BANKING. capPct was Math.min(100, Math.round(totalMins / 480 * 100)) and that single value fed BOTH the progress bar's width AND the percentage a person reads - so a 12-hour plan against an 8-hour day rendered 'Capacity 100% - 12.0h / 8h', the hours saying 150% and the percentage saying 100%, contradicting each other in one row. findings.detail: THE V2 SUBJECT IS UNREACHABLE, AND THE REASON IS A DEFECT ON THIS PAGE - not a limitation of the probe. Clicking the page's own '+ Schedule' control (the element carrying onclick="openAddModal()") leaves #modal with computed **visibility: hidden** at both 390 and 1280 CSS px, so nothing appears. Zero console errors and zero page errors, so nothing threw: the open path runs to completion and still produces an invisible dialog. THE MECHANISM, READ FROM THE CASCADE ITSELF rather than inferred. Two rules govern it: `.sheet-overlay:not(.open), .modal-overlay:not(.open) { visibility: hidden; transition: opacity 0.25s, visibility linear 0.25s; }` and `.sheet-overlay.open, .modal-overlay.open { visibility: visible; transition-delay: 0s; }`. Visibility is therefore gated on an **`.open`** class. After the click, #modal's className is exactly `"modal-overlay"` - the `hidden` class has been removed and `display` has become `flex`, but `.open` is NEVER ADDED. There is no inline style. So the element has layout (measured 367x1275, with #modal-box at 367x569) and is invisible. IT IS A CONTRACT MISMATCH, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN PATCHING: the page's opener uses the OLD protocol - remove `.hidden`, set `display` - while the SHARED overlay CSS moved to an `.open` protocol. Pages whose openers were updated still work: inventory's #part-modal and logbook's #asset-modal both opened and were fully measurable in this same pass, and community's #thread-overlay and project-manager's #modal-wizard likewise. dayplanner was left behind. WHAT IT COSTS A PERSON: '+ Schedule' is the primary way to add an item to a day plan. The button responds, the page does not change, and there is no error - the most confusing possible failure, because nothing tells the user to try something else. Any other page using `.modal-overlay` with an un-migrated opener has the same bug, so the fix should be verified across every `.modal-overlay` / `.sheet-overlay` opener rather than only here. NOT MEASURED, DELIBERATELY: this row's own oracle (the V2 layout/state/visual contract) cannot be measured while the view cannot be reached, and a pass over an invisible dialog would be a false green - the exact shape this bank refuses. The row therefore stays OWED with the blocker named, and becomes measurable the moment the opener adds `.open`. TO FINISH (batched per A15, and it is one line): have openAddModal() add the `open` class to #modal - or better, route it through whatever shared helper the migrated pages use, so the next CSS contract change does not strand it again. Then walk dayplanner's V2 rows.

findings.detail: THE V2 SUBJECT IS UNREACHABLE, AND THE REASON IS A DEFECT ON THIS PAGE - not a limitation of the probe. Clicking the page's own '+ Schedule' control (the element carrying onclick="openAddModal()") leaves #modal with computed **visibility: hidden** at both 390 and 1280 CSS px, so nothing appears. Zero console errors and zero page errors, so nothing threw: the open path runs to completion and still produces an invisible dialog. THE MECHANISM, READ FROM THE CASCADE ITSELF rather than inferred. Two rules govern it: `.sheet-overlay:not(.open), .modal-overlay:not(.open) { visibility: hidden; transition: opacity 0.25s, visibility linear 0.25s; }` and `.sheet-overlay.open, .modal-overlay.open { visibility: visible; transition-delay: 0s; }`. Visibility is therefore gated on an **`.open`** class. After the click, #modal's className is exactly `"modal-overlay"` - the `hidden` class has been removed and `display` has become `flex`, but `.open` is NEVER ADDED. There is no inline style. So the element has layout (measured 367x1275, with #modal-box at 367x569) and is invisible. IT IS A CONTRACT MISMATCH, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN PATCHING: the page's opener uses the OLD protocol - remove `.hidden`, set `display` - while the SHARED overlay CSS moved to an `.open` protocol. Pages whose openers were updated still work: inventory's #part-modal and logbook's #asset-modal both opened and were fully measurable in this same pass, and community's #thread-overlay and project-manager's #modal-wizard likewise. dayplanner was left behind. WHAT IT COSTS A PERSON: '+ Schedule' is the primary way to add an item to a day plan. The button responds, the page does not change, and there is no error - the most confusing possible failure, because nothing tells the user to try something else. Any other page using `.modal-overlay` with an un-migrated opener has the same bug, so the fix should be verified across every `.modal-overlay` / `.sheet-overlay` opener rather than only here. NOT MEASURED, DELIBERATELY: this row's own oracle (the V2 layout/state/visual contract) cannot be measured while the view cannot be reached, and a pass over an invisible dialog would be a false green - the exact shape this bank refuses. The row therefore stays OWED with the blocker named, and becomes measurable the moment the opener adds `.open`. TO FINISH (batched per A15, and it is one line): have openAddModal() add the `open` class to #modal - or better, route it through whatever shared helper the migrated pages use, so the next CSS contract change does not strand it again. Then walk dayplanner's V2 rows.

findings.detail: FAILS, NARROWLY AND SPECIFICALLY: **1 of 9** controls in the dialog presents an activation target under 44x44 CSS px, at exactly **32px** tall (height histogram {32: 1}). Measured on the ACTIVATION target - inputs resolve to closest('label') where one exists - so this is not an input being measured instead of its label. ONE control rather than a systemic problem, which is worth stating plainly: the other 8 clear the floor, so this is a single element 12px short rather than a density choice applied across the form. It still matters - this dialog is filled on a phone, and a 32px target next to full-size ones is the one a thumb misses - but it is a one-element fix, not a redesign. THE BLOCKER RECORDED ON THIS PAGE'S V2 ROWS IS FIXED, VERIFIED, AND THAT IS WHY THIS ROW IS MEASURABLE. WHAT WAS BROKEN: clicking the page's own '+ Schedule' control left #modal at computed visibility:hidden at both 390 and 1280 CSS px - layout present (367x1275, #modal-box 367x569), nothing on screen, and ZERO console or page errors. The most confusing possible failure: the button responds, the page does not change, and nothing tells the user to try something else. '+ Schedule' is the primary way to add an item to a day plan. THE MECHANISM, READ FROM THE CASCADE: two shared rules govern the overlay - `.sheet-overlay:not(.open), .modal-overlay:not(.open) { visibility: hidden; transition: opacity 0.25s, visibility linear 0.25s }` and `.sheet-overlay.open, .modal-overlay.open { visibility: visible }`. Visibility is gated on `.open`. But dayplanner's openers used the OLDER protocol - remove `.hidden`, set display - so after the click the className was exactly 'modal-overlay' and `.open` was never added. A CONTRACT MISMATCH between the page's JS and the shared CSS, not a logic error, which is why nothing threw. PAGES WHOSE OPENERS HAD MIGRATED STILL WORKED, which is what localised it: inventory's #part-modal, logbook's #asset-modal, community's #thread-overlay and project-manager's #modal-wizard all opened and measured cleanly in the same pass. dayplanner was the one left behind. THE FIX - THREE EDITS, SYMMETRIC, COVERING EVERY SITE: `.classList.add('open')` in openAddModal (dayplanner .html:1719) AND in the edit-path opener (:1740) - there were TWO openers, and fixing only the one the button calls would have left editing an existing item broken - plus `.classList.remove('open')` in closeModal, because an overlay left with `.open` behind `hidden` would transition from the wrong state on the next open. VERIFIED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: after the click, className 'modal-overlay open', computed visibility VISIBLE, and the dialog reads 'Schedule Item / Title * / Date * / Start Time / End Time / Category / Preventive Maintenance...' - i.e. a real, readable form rather than a box with layout. After closeModal: 'modal-overlay hidden', visibility hidden, display none. Zero page errors either way. The settle was a waitForFunction on visibility becoming visible AND every control inside losing visibility:hidden, not a fixed sleep - an earlier reading of this same modal was taken mid-state and reported controls:0 alongside formControls:6, which is the signature of measuring an unsettled view.

findings.detail: FAILS: 175 of 175 effective tap targets inside #calendar-wrap are under the platform's own 44px floor - div.wilo-day-header wh-kbd-a11y 39.3x51.4 via own box; div.wilo-day-header wh-kbd-a11y 39.3x51.4 via own box; div.wilo-day-header wh-kbd-a11y 39.3x51.4 via own box; div.wilo-day-header today wh-kbd 39.3x51.4 via own box; div.wilo-day-header wh-kbd-a11y 39.3x51.4 via own box. THIS IS MEASURED ON THE SAME RULER THAT PASSED 750 of 750 AT PAGE LEVEL: the rule is ported verbatim from the V1 prover, so these are controls the platform's own standard would reject, in a view V1 never opened.  HOW IT WAS MEASURED, and why these rows sat owed for so long: CJ was measured platform-wide at V1 and banked there, and V2/V3 stayed owed for ONE reason - nobody could open those views. Resolving all 15 dialog open paths (each read from SOURCE, never matched by label) removed that blocker, and the same measurements now run inside the OPENED dialog. The open-path table lives in tools/dialog_targets.mjs, shared with the modal-exit prover so the two cannot drift apart. SCOPED TO THE DIALOG, NOT THE PAGE, which is the whole point: a dialog OVERLAYS the page, so measuring document.body with a sheet open would re-measure V1 and bank it as V2 - the one-reading-for-every-layer error this bank has already paid for once. Every measurement is rooted at the dialog element. Overflow compares each visible descendant's right edge against the dialog's own content box, with a 1px tolerance (an earlier arc counted a 0.109px abutment as occlusion) and honours overflow-x auto/scroll/hidden/clip on an ancestor INSIDE the dialog, because a deliberately scrollable panel is not a defect. THE TAP-TARGET RULE IS PORTED VERBATIM FROM THE V1 PROVER, NOT REINVENTED, and that correction is why this number means anything. The first cut omitted four of V1's exclusions - sr-only, disabled, the actionable check, and the WCAG 2.5.5 inline-link-in-prose exception - and REPLACED a control's rect with its label instead of UNIONING them. Applying a stricter standard at V2 than at V1 does not find defects, it manufactures a difference between the two views and calls it one. With V1's exact rule restored the count came back IDENTICAL, which is what makes these findings real rather than an artifact: they are measured on the same ruler that banked 750/750 at page level. SCOPE: overflow is measured at THREE widths - 390, 641 and 1280 - and each width's row is banked from its OWN reading, never spread from one width to the others. The dialog is not closed between widths; two animation frames are awaited after each resize so the panel has actually reflowed, and a zero width at ANY width fails the whole target rather than quietly trusting the rest. TAP TARGETS are measured at 390 only - that is the mobile-first floor the V1 prover used, and a control that clears 44px at 390 does not shrink as the viewport grows. Two of the 15 dialogs are UNGRADED with their reason recorded rather than counted: resume's #review-sheet has no read-only path in (it needs the upload -> resume-extract pipeline, which WRITES) and hive's #handover-sheet cannot be reached at all. The walk is NON-WRITING - it opens a dialog, measures, and presses Escape.
